questions.enonce_markdown:
Outline the drawbacks of a barter system of exchange and explain how they have been removed by the following functions of money:

(i) Medium of exchange

(ii) Measure of value

(iii) Store of value

(iv) Standard of deferred payment

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** **Barter** is the direct exchange of goods and services for other goods and services, without using money. It works in a small community, but it has serious drawbacks. Money was introduced to remove them, and each function of money answers one drawback.

**(i) Medium of exchange (2 marks)**

- *Drawback of barter:* **lack of a double coincidence of wants**. A farmer who has maize and wants a pair of shoes must find a shoemaker who wants maize at that very moment. The search is long and costly. Barter also suffers from **indivisibility**: a cow cannot be cut up to buy a bag of salt.
- *How money removes it:* money is **generally accepted** in payment for any good or service. The farmer sells his maize for FCFA to any buyer, then uses the FCFA to buy shoes from any shoemaker. Selling and buying are separated, and small FCFA notes and coins make payment of any amount possible.

**(ii) Measure of value (2 marks)**

- *Drawback of barter:* **no common measure of value**. Every good has to be priced in terms of every other good (1 goat = 3 bags of rice = 10 chickens...). With $n$ goods there are $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ exchange rates, for example $\frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10$ rates for only 5 goods. Comparing values is confusing.
- *How money removes it:* money is a **unit of account**. Each good has **one price in FCFA** (5 goods need only 5 prices), so values are easy to compare, to add up and to record in accounts and budgets.

**(iii) Store of value (2 marks)**

- *Drawback of barter:* **difficulty of storing wealth**. Wealth kept in the form of goods such as tomatoes, fish or livestock is **perishable**, bulky, costly to keep and may lose value.
- *How money removes it:* money keeps its **purchasing power over time** (when prices are reasonably stable), takes little space and is easy to keep safely, for example in a bank account. A trader can sell today and spend the money next month.

**(iv) Standard of deferred payment (2 marks)**

- *Drawback of barter:* **difficulty of credit and future payments**. A debt to be repaid in goods in the future is hard to define (what quality? what quantity? what if the good becomes scarce?). This discourages lending.
- *How money removes it:* money is the unit in which **debts and future payments** are stated (a loan of 500,000 FCFA is repaid in FCFA, with interest). Credit, loans, rents, wages and instalment purchases become easy.

**Conclusion.** Money therefore removes the main weaknesses of barter and makes trade, saving and credit easier.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Differentiate between "demand for money" and "supply of money". (4 marks)

(ii) Why do people in an economy prefer to hold money in liquid form? (8 marks)

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Demand for money and supply of money (4 marks)**

| | **Demand for money** | **Supply of money** |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | The **amount of money that people and firms want to hold** (keep in cash or in easily spendable form) at a given time. It is the desire to hold **liquid** assets. | The **total stock of money in circulation** in the economy at a given time: notes and coins plus bank deposits that can be spent. |
| Who decides | Households, firms and the government, according to their needs and motives. | Mainly the **central bank** and the commercial banks (through note issue and credit creation). |
| Determined by | Income level, price level, interest rate, habits and expectations. | Government and central bank policy, the reserves of banks and the credit they create. |
| Example | A trader decides to keep 200,000 FCFA in cash for the week's purchases. | The central bank puts more notes into circulation or banks grant more loans. |

In short, demand for money is what people **wish to hold**, while supply of money is what the monetary authorities and banks **make available**.

**(ii) Why people prefer to hold money in liquid form (8 marks)**

**Liquidity** is the ease and speed with which an asset can be turned into **goods and services without loss of value**. **Money (cash) is the most liquid asset.** People hold it for the following reasons (the three motives of liquidity preference):

1. **Transactions motive (2 marks).** Households and firms need cash for **day-to-day purchases**, such as food, transport, school fees, wages and raw materials. Income is received at intervals (monthly or weekly) but spending is continuous, so some money must be held in hand.
2. **Precautionary motive (2 marks).** People keep cash for **unexpected needs** such as illness, accidents, funerals or the repair of a machine. Cash can be used **immediately** to meet an emergency.
3. **Speculative motive (2 marks).** People keep money ready to take advantage of **profitable opportunities**: to buy goods, land or shares when prices fall, or to avoid the loss of value of other assets (for example when the price of a financial asset is expected to fall).
4. **General acceptability and no cost of conversion (2 marks).** Money is **accepted everywhere** and in every transaction. Other assets such as land, houses, livestock or machines may take time to sell, may need a buyer to be found and may be sold at a loss, whereas money can be spent at once at its **full value**.

**Conclusion.** The advantage of liquidity is security and flexibility. The cost is that cash earns **no interest**, so people balance liquidity against the interest they could earn on other assets.
